utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to all. May I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Tom Hannis with Crispian Smith on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Deirdre Montgomery, and Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have a matter, Mr. Zecevic, before the witness takes the stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, before the witness arrives, we were instructed by the Trial Chamber to expedite our response in relation to the motion to amend the Rule 65 ter list filed by the Prosecution sometime ago. And we are informing the Trial Chamber that we are not objecting to it. So thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After careful and detailed consideration, Your Honours, we do not have objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trbojevic. I would, before I invite Mr. Zecevic to continue his cross-examination, remind you that you are still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, before we begin there's just something that I would like to clear up. Yesterday in the course of my questioning, on page 4.162, line 20, and 4.163, line 1, if you recall, we discussed the attempts of the Serb side to block within the institutions of the system the request for the declaration of independence [Realtime transcript read in error "incompetent dependence"] of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you said then that such possibilities were more than limited, or rather, non-existent; but that in spite of that, the president, Alija Izetbegovic would have signed such a document and sent it to the international community, to which I ask whether he would have done that without the approval of the Assembly and you confirmed that. Do you recall our exchange on that topic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the reason I'm asking is because on these pages that I've mentioned, in the transcript is says that such a document would have been signed by the speaker of the parliament of the Assembly, but that's of course not true because the president of the parliament, or the Assembly, was Mr. Krajisnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not correct because we were discussing this within our group, how to actually postpone the vote on this, and whether we would ask or call for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or maybe not. And something that I omitted to mention yesterday was that one the topics emerged was that we should actually address this issue to the army command, at the time it was still the Yugoslav People's Army, so that it could within its obligations, legal obligations, intervene in order to prevent such a signing of a document that the president of the Presidency, Mr. Izetbegovic, would sign without the approval of the Assembly. And on that occasion, Karadzic said that he could not go and see General Djurdjevac, if I recall correctly, he was the commander of the 2nd Military District, that he couldn't go there and ask that of Djurdjevac because he was one of the leaders of a national parties which, as far as the JNA was concerned, still were not fully legitimate, as it were. So he could not really expect any kind of support from them as for this position of the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just two things here, please. So when we talked yesterday, you said that the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, would sign that document and send it to the international community, or rather, would have signed it and sent it to the international community without the approval of the Assembly if that situation should arise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was our assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And you said here that Karadzic told you that he could not really take this up with General Djurdjevac, and if I understood you correctly, Karadzic said that he could not influence in any way the Yugoslav People's Army, or rather, General Djurdjevac, because General Djurdjevac did not support, as it were, the positions of nationalist or ethnic parties because he was a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, which was ideologically opposed to the SDS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, just a small thing regarding the transcript. On page 2, line 16, the transcript has come out to say that: "We discussed the attempts of the Serb side to block within the institutions of the system the request for the declaration of incompetent dependence," I think the witness said "independence."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I wasn't following the transcript in full. [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let's resume. Mr. Trbojevic, thank you for this clarification. Now, you recall that on the 17th of June, 1992, an operative plan of the army -- of the government was adopted. Do you remember that? Or a plan of work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall that I remember the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But do you recall that it was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was some work done in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please pull up 1D00-552 on the screens, and perhaps the usher could help us and pass on to Mr. Trbojevic this document in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a cover letter dated 17th July 1992, signed by the government secretary, Mr. Lakicevic. This is a document from the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it's a cover letter with the plan of work for the measures in order to prevent the disruption in conditions in a state of war, and then ministries are called upon to give their own proposals and suggestions, and a dead-line of the 20th of July is given. For the transcript, just to say that it was signed by Mr. Nedeljko Lakic. I misread the last name. So this is correct, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please pull up the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the second page, this is the title page of this document, we see again that we have the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the government, an operative programme of measures to prevent social disruption in conditions of a state of war. And perhaps by error, or rather, the error was probably in the cover letter, but the date here is the 17th of June, 1992. In any case it's either June or July. Do you recall when this came about approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really recall anymore the work that we did on this programme, but it begins with constitution amendments. And, you know, would you just pose the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just wanted to see if we could determine the exact date, but since you mentioned that these are constitutional amendments, I assume that it would rather be June than July?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really recall when we did this work, and I'm not claiming that this was actually adopted, because the Law on Territorial Organisation was never on the agenda, although it was constantly being discussed how districts should be set up and so on. But that never came to light actually, so that President Djeric, the prime minister, asked me on a couple of occasions why that hadn't been followed through, but, well, that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please take a look at page 3 -- or rather, 4 of this document. In B/C/S that's page 2 in your hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under item 3, we see that there is a decree on delineating or establishing border crossings and organising customs control and, among other things, this is the responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior. Now, the day before yesterday when you were questioned by my learned friend Mr. Hannis, he put to you a number of government conclusions that related specifically to this matter, the establishment of border crossings and organisation of customs control. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do know that we discussed this need, that this was a necessity to establish a service that will check all the goods that are imported and exported out of the country, in other words, customs control, so that we could actually have an operational authority there, that it could function, and I recall that we appointed as director or perhaps acting director of this republic customs office, a certain --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I know he did not accept this but how it actually transpired in the end I don't know. I couldn't tell you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But do you remember that there were certain comments made by Mr. Stanisic in government sessions? You were shown some documents in that respect yesterday that dealt with, among other things, the setting of up of the customs or, rather, border service; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that this setting up establishment of border crossings, in other words, the establishment of the border police was actually set up and that it started their work on some of the border crossings in Republika Srpska in the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that we made some decisions as to which places will be the future border crossings. This was probably within the competence of the Ministry of the Interior to actually man those border crossings, to provide the physical control there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can now take a look at page 5 in e-court. On your hard copy, that will be page 3. Items 8 and 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This relates to the drafting of wartime organisation and systemisation, development of wartime organisation and specification of jobs. And it says all ministries, other republic organs and organisations and state agencies are to draft their wartime organisation and specification of jobs implying a transition to wartime operation. And then in parenthesis it says determining the minimum number of employees needed for good performance and so on and so forth, and there is mention here of a war commission or commissions. Now, do you recall that this drafting of the wartime organisation and specification of jobs had been a strict legal obligation in the former Yugoslavia under the Law on the Self-Defence -- on All People's Defence and --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a schematic of jobs which have to function in crisis situation up to mobilisation spots and relocation of companies, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I presume that this was the basis for this obligation for all the ministries and why it found its way in the operative programme of the government of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one on the one hand; but on the other hand you have the duty of the people to be -- to heed the call-up, mobilisation call-up. Sometimes you never knew who would show up for work and who would show up for mobilisation. And this is why organisations had to determine this matter so that the army could know who is going to stay behind to work in an organisation or in a company and who is going to show up at mobilisation spots.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The next I'd like to show you is page 8 in e-court and that would be page 6 in your copy. Item 18. It goes for an obligation under this operative programme to draft rules on internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior in wartime conditions. And under that heading it says: "Internal organisation" it means the Ministry of the Interior, "needs to be adjusted to the purview and tasks in wartime conditions, namely: Protection and physical securing of installations of special importance to defence, and protection, and then control of movements across the state borders, personal security," et cetera, et cetera, all the tasks as laid down by law and that is envisaged as an obligation of the Ministry of the Interior. You recall that at several occasions, the government got reported by the Ministry of the Interior on how they were working on these rules of internal organisation in -- the first draft which was sent to centres of public security was dated beginning of September 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle I recall that there were discussions about that. This is the same thing as the previous matter that we discussed. This is just customary and usual matter to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a voluminous document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Somebody must have gathered drafts and proposals from all of the ministries, maybe drafting the government law and then listed all the ministries quoting the obligations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the rules of internal organisation of the MUP, this is a voluminous and lengthy document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's look up page 9 in e-court. It would be page 7 in your version, in your hard copy. Items 21 and 22. As you can see, item 21 deals with: "Order to take off the road any motor vehicle without proper documentation." I think that yesterday we discussed that there was an instruction and a conclusion of the government to this effect. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this request that an order be issued to take such vehicles off the road is a repetition of something which is enshrined in law. There's no possibility in law for a vehicle without proof of title and without proper insurance to be used on roads. This is one of the usual tasks of the Ministry of Interior to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, item 22: "Decision on an ex-territorial principle organising active-duty police force." I think that we commented a document yesterday dated November, and you confirmed that the influence of local organs on members of the MUP was a huge problem, and obviously a huge problem for the ministry. And now it reads, under 22: "Due to the demonstrated extreme susceptibility of municipal organs of Internal Affairs to the influence of local authorities and family connections, it is necessary to establish criteria according to which only a minimum number of employees of a police station may be natives of the given locality." First of all, let me ask you: Do you recall this problem that we discussed yesterday, and that problem dating from 1992, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall, and when this is -- concerned police workers in local police stations were predominantly inhabitants of that municipality. People living in that local community and by function and in terms of their remit, they were connected with the Ministry of the Interior. But people from Sarajevo or some other places could not work in other parts of the country, most of them were locals. They worked where they lived. And this is one of the interpretations of this problem and that the author of this was not quite familiar with this situation, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 10, item 23 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Trbojevic, that would be page 8 in your hard copy. Goes for: "Operative programme of activities to secure the prerequisite for efficient functioning of the Internal Affairs service." And the Ministry of the Interior is obliged to co-operate with the Ministry of Justice and Ministry of Defence. What I'm interested in in particular is paragraph 3 of this item, that would be on the next page in the English version, first paragraph on the page, which reads: "Within the framework of its activities, the ministry and its services should make a special provision for an organised approach to work related to data collection and processing, and the documentation and genocide perpetrated against the civilian population." Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, in this document under item 21, there is no mention --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Item 23, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There's no mention of war crimes and genocide perpetrated against no particular group, but any perpetrators and the victims coming from any ethnic group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then last page, page 22 in the e-court, item 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That would be the last page, page 20 in your hard copy, item 66. It is an "order to establish a state commission to investigate extreme cases of theft and other abuses." And it reads: "Establish an interdepartmental commission made up of representatives of the Ministry of Interior, Ministry of Justice, and the responsible department, which would conduct investigations based on reports received by the MUP." This would be in -- this item of the operative programme and plan is in keeping with what we discussed in terms of the government's conclusions that have been sent to ministries on several occasions in terms of TAS abuses, concerning oil, et cetera. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This is something which went a long time. There were cases of procurement of oil worth millions of Deutschemarks and there were questions who took the money. The Golf vehicles from TAS were the most prominent example and they were at the forefront.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you correctly, you think that this is a working material, working document and that you are not sure whether it's been -- it was ever adopted by the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a working document but I'm not sure. I don't know whether it was adopted in its entirety, but what I'm sure about is that there was discussion about this and the ministries tried to work along these lines, since these are legal obligations of each of those ministries mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, all those ministries performed tasks and duties mentioned in this operative plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was an initiative which was sent to the organs. Whether it was adopted in this form or in an amended form, that's what I'm not sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you saw page 1 and Nedeljko Lakic's signature. Do you recall his signature?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a graphologist but it does look like his signature, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to submit this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My only objection, and maybe it just goes to weight, really deals with there are a number of handwritten notations in the original about whether something is completed or pending or question marks, et cetera. I don't think this witness is able to help us with who wrote those and when they wrote them. So with that understanding, I guess I don't object but I think that is something that you'll have to take in mind when considering this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It seems to me that it follows a matter of course, the Chamber would have to take note of that. So the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D96, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Trbojevic, I cannot recall, but I believe it was the day before yesterday, maybe it was yesterday, Mr. Hannis showed you a document, P233, minutes from a government session, where it stated that the government ordered Mr. Mico Stanisic to determine and establish the security situation at Bijeljina. Do you recall commenting that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I found the reference, that would be pages 4099 and 4100, dating the day before yesterday. I would like to show you a document which is connected with the establishment of the situation in Bijeljina. I believe that my learned colleague asked you about those facts, but he didn't show you any documents. It is 65 ter document 194. It is a document of the Ministry of the Interior, Centre of Security Service of Bijeljina, dated 29th of July, 1992. It is signed by the then head of the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could ask Mr. Usher to give Mr. Trbojevic a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document was sent to the president of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Radovan Karadzic. You see the first page?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think I responded to -- replied to the Prosecutor that I had not seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2, please. It's starting with a heading "Information," and it reads: "Information on the involvement and activities of the Ministry of Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in establishing authority and the Rule of Law in the area covered by the Centre for Security Services Bijeljina." And it -- that document, Mr. Andan explains what had happened between the 27th of June, 1992, when an expert team of the MUP, of the Ministry of the Interior, of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina arrived to Bijeljina. Can you see that? That would be on page 2 and page 3 in e-court, and in your hard copy, first and second page, the orientation would be this 27th of June, 1992, for you. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, this end of June corresponds to the request and the government's conclusion sent to Mico Stanisic instructing him to establish the situation in Bijeljina, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond. Prosecutor asked me whether Stanisic went to Bijeljina. I answered that I did not know that, but Andan now reports that he went to Bijeljina. I'm not sure whether this is the same action or not, but it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, the last document, page 6 in e-court, and page 5 in your hard copy. The penultimate paragraph, which reads: "Finally, to complete the picture, we must stress that there were fierce opposition and resistance to the involvement of the expert team of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of BiH, not only verbal but also armed. For example, some members of the expert team were threatened with execution, various misinformation was put into circulation and lies were spread about the alleged on-site activities and the rule of terror of the expert team in the field, protest rallies against the 'newcomers' were organised, and three unsuccessful attacks against the CSB building with heavy weapons were carried out in order to seize the building and banish the expert team of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of BiH." Mr. Trbojevic, you read what is stated here and what Mr. Dragan Andan, chief of the security services centre, wrote. Are you familiar with those incidents of armed attacks with heavy weapons against the building of the CSB centre.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, sir, would you please read the very last portion, the very last sentence in the document. It's handwritten. And I believe this is Mr. Radovan Karadzic's signature. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Keep enforcing order and the rule of law, Radovan Karadzic." This resembles his signature. It looks like his own signature that I had occasion to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. But in any case, it arises from this document that the Ministry of the Interior again acted according to the conclusions ever the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that this witness was unable to authenticate this document or recognise it, I propose that it be MFI'd because, if I recall, Mr. Andan is on the witness list of the Prosecution and we will probably have occasion to put this document to him when he comes to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine, but actually based on my prior understandings, I have no reason to doubt the authenticity. I don't object to admitting it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Even better. Thank you very much, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Tendered, marked and admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D97, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, you said something to this effect during your evidence, about in July, approximately at that time, the Ministry of the Interior set up its seat, its headquarters in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was transferred to Bijeljina. I can't tell you the exact date, but about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in fact, it was only in Bijeljina that the Ministry of the Interior began to operate normally, if I may use that term, as some time toward the end of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the fact that they actually all came together in a central building, there were finally conditions for normal work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that from mid-July and on, the Ministry of the Interior held so-called collegium meetings with all the chiefs of Security Services Centre every month, all of those who could actually attend?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did hear of these collegium meetings and I heard of that being the ministry's usual mode of work. I never attended one of those, but I know that this was common knowledge. They discussed in these meetings important issues that related to the ministry itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that the Ministry of the Interior dispatched inspectors from the headquarters to conduct inspections and provide instructions to Security Services Centres and some public security stations, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I assume then that you are not aware either that these inspectors, after they completed these inspections, they would also conduct checks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Ministry of the Interior, in the course of 1992, adopted a number of significant rules of work and instructions that was -- were necessitated by their work, or were necessary for their work; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that I know about that, but if they were published in the Official Gazettes, then I probably had occasion to see them. But I can't really recall. I remember that there was some work done on the Law on Citizenship and there was some work that I participated in personally, but as for the rules of service, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware of a document called: "The instruction on the urgent, current and occasional reporting, statistical reporting in Ministry of the Interior organs," dated October 1992? This is document 1D51, an exhibit already. I will show it to you and perhaps you will recognise it. Have you heard of this document, this instruction?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please assist. Please let Mr. Trbojevic see this document. Maybe that will help him refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let me then just read out to you in view of the fact that you haven't seen this document, but maybe you've heard of these things. Have you heard of a document entitled: "Instruction Issued in 1992: An instruction on the rules of conduct of MUP members." And as a reference, this was Exhibit 1D50 in this case. Have you heard ever of such a document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, have you ever heard of the binding instruction during conducting searches? For reference purposes, that's 1D52.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a document entitled: "Instructions on the methods on preparing annual reports"? For your reference, this is 1D53.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that the ministry adopted the rules on disciplinary responsibility in a state of imminent threat of war and in a state of war? This was Exhibit 1D54 in this case.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I know that -- well, I can't say that I know that such rules have been adopted, but I do know that there was work done on drafting rules, both in the army and in the police. And I know that I participated at the request of the Ministry of Defence in one such group who worked on that, but how the thing was done within the police, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that there was some work done in that direction in order to actually adopt such rules; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We discussed a few minutes earlier, the rules on the internal organisation of MUP in a state of imminent threat of war and in a state of war, and this has to do with the operative plan of the government, item 18. In this case, this is document 65 ter 248, a draft of those rules. You said that you remember, recall, that the rules were drafted, but do you remember whether you ever actually had it in your hands?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I believe that it was adopted because it would be very unlikely that such a document wouldn't be adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was only adopted in early 1993 because of the government ousting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Ministry of the Interior adopted a binding -- Witness, your response was not recorded in the transcript, Mr. Trbojevic. When I said that these rules were adopted practically in early 1993 because the government had, in the meantime, the government which you were the vice-president of, had been ousted, you said something.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really say anything specific. I had already said before that, to me, it would seem highly unlikely that such a document wouldn't be adopted. Now, the fact that a few months had elapsed between its drafting and adoption, now that's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Are you aware that the Ministry of the Interior adopted a binding instruction on documenting war crimes? For reference this is document 1D63. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, but I do know that all the discussions on that issue implied that the documents and information should be obtained and from and provided by the police, because this was part of their work, collecting evidence and documents on crimes committed, so that any further discussion of that matter would proceed from that premise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This was an obligation that the police had under the Law on the Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You recall that the Ministry of the Interior submitted on a number of occasions information on the current security situation, this information was reported to the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that already on the 31st of May, 1992, such a report was submitted, such a report on the current security situation. For reference purposes, that's Exhibit P221. This is a document -- actually, government minutes. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really confirm specifically because I can't tell you which of those reports I saw -- I have seen, but I do know that there were reports and there was information that was interesting to read for one's own enlightenment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to show you document 65 ter 176. That's a document coming from the Ministry of the Interior entitled "Information," a report submitted both to the president of the government, or the prime minister, and the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please help us with a hard copy. The document bears the date 17th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis asked you something about this document. I believe that you said that you do not remember seeing this document, but let me show it to you again because one of the questions of Mr. Hannis's was a question about the report on the work of the state security service, if you remember. Do you remember that? Do you remember that question that Mr. Hannis put to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis asked you, the day before yesterday, about the government conclusion in which the government sought a report on the work of the state security service, and then he asked you whether you remember ever receiving such a report, and you said that you couldn't confirm that you -- but that you recall that there were a number of reports from the Ministry of the Interior but you couldn't remember this particular one.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the only thing that I can repeat now. I know that there were such reports. There was some information in such reports that I hadn't heard of before, but what those reports were or how they were entitled, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me now, now that you've looked at this report entitled: Information on certain aspects of work done to date and the tasks ahead, can you tell us, do you remember this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see. I would have to look through the content. The subject matter was a general matter that was discussed -- being discussed in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, just for your reference, perhaps I can show you page 9 in e-court of the B/C/S version, the last paragraph, and in your case that's on page 9. It's page 10 in the English version. And it says here the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page in e-court, please. Page 9, B/C/S; 10 in English. The last paragraph. Just a moment. In English that will be on page 6, in the last paragraph, in e-court. Page 6. I apologise, on page 6 that's not the last paragraph but, rather, the second from the top, beginning with the words: "Preventing and documenting war crimes ..." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see it this document, Mr. Trbojevic, beginning with the words: "Preventing and documenting war crimes"? The B/C/S copy is perhaps a bit illegible, but can you find that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can actually make it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it reads: "Prevention and documenting war crimes by using all legally prescribed methods of documenting such activities," et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, and it reads that this was one of the priorities of the National Security Service or state security service and public security service. Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall that. My recollection is quite the opposite to this claim that it was a priority. In attempts to establish a commission to investigation war crimes and what the extent for the co-operation of the institute for investigating war crimes from Belgrade, I did not have an impression that out on the field we encountered a welcoming reception in the local public security stations whenever we showed up. To the contrary, we were being ignored. There was no will on their part to co-operate. So what is written here, that this was their priority, I do not believe to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall an action that the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, conducted in Zvornik in July 1992 to arrest the Yellow Wasps paramilitary group and to process those war crimes? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall the existence of that group, some meetings with it, and when it was crushed. And those meetings with them were less than savoury. Whenever I encountered them, these were not savoury occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, what I presented to you yesterday and today as examples in connection with what the Ministry of the Interior was dealing with at the time, could you and will you agree with me that it inevitably follows from all of that that the ministry acted in keeping with the operative plan and the instructions and orders of the government; isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that for the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I mean, that conflict between Mr. Stanisic and Prime Minister Djeric, did not influence to that extent the conduct and activities of the ministry as part of that government, the Ministry of the Interior as part of that government, in fulfilling the duties and obligations that the Ministry of the Interior has under the act on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reaction of Stanisic towards Djeric could not have influenced the relations between Stanisic and other parts of the Ministry of the Interior. I'm not sure whether it had an influence in terms of his relationships towards and with the organs and in the collegium meetings, whatever you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Collegiums.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in connection with his centres for security service, I don't think that Djeric tried to do anything against him or to interfere and I have no knowledge that anything happened in that vein as a consequence of them not being on friendly terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Having regard to the fact that all those normative acts were prepared by the Ministry of the Interior in 1992, some of which are undoubtedly key for the functioning of that ministry, it could be concluded that the ministry, to a great extent, fulfilled what would be expected of it at that stage of the ministry's being setting up?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with your assessment. I cannot pin-point a percentage, maybe 90 per cent, but the -- it was obvious that the present infrastructure functioned much better than in other walks of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say it functioned better than in other segments of the society, do you mean by that some of the ministries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The setting up of the army and the setting up of all organs and authorities, from municipal authorities to ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that at the end of your examination-in-chief, Mr. Hannis showed you this document, P400. It's an exhibit and it is a transcript of the Assembly of the Serbian people, dated 23rd and 24th November, 1992. On page 55 of that document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can have it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have a hard copy for you. I believe that it would be easier for you to follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like you to show me page 55 in both the Serbian and the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Minister Subotic speaks and at that Assembly he took part in debate, and he said that he will take responsibility for failing to set up the Ministry of Defence by that point, that he'd managed to find only six people for -- do you recall his intervention?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not, but I did discuss matters with Minister Subotic and I was aware that the situation in that ministry was substandard or inappropriate, that only a handful of people worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you are, in fact, aware of the situation at that ministry that Mr. Subotic explained and described at this Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The army as an armed force had its command and control, and set up structures, and the Ministry of Defence was lame, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Trbojevic, while we are discussing this document, a digression, you recall that you took the floor at that Assembly; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your speech is at page 45. You have pagination marks in the top right-hand corner. I'm interested in --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have page 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The transcript number. Midway through the document, page 45. There are two days covered by this document, day one, day two. Towards the bottom of page 45, the last paragraph, you say, you address the Assembly, you say: "You've all, I believe, heard that Vitomir Zepinic became an officer of military security. I will wonder, and I'm still wondering why." Please tell me, your learning that Mr. Vitomir Zepinic becoming an officer in the military security, can you recall that and can you tell us more about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my speech I continue, it reads, the minister of defence, our minister of the interior informed us, I heard that that person was arrested. And from the Ministry of Defence I heard that the General Staff of our army, in there nobody knows why he was employed. I have no prejudice but I -- it is intolerable that the minister of defence doesn't know who is employed by his ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at page 47 in English. I apologise for being late with this reference, that would be page 47 in English. That would be second paragraph, it states "Zapinic" in English but it's supposed to be "Zepinic."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify a couple of things here. So you learned that Mr. Zepinic was arrested, and if I understood you correctly, after being arrested, he suddenly shows up in the Army of Republika Srpska as a military security officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Zepinic, I believe, was assistant minister or deputy minister of the interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a Serbian cadre. When we went our separate ways, Zepinic remained in Sarajevo and he was arrested when he emerged from Sarajevo. He was interrogated. We heard his answers on TV. He was suspect collaborator with the Muslims. After a while, he showed up in the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Defence did not know that he had been employed within that ministry. And it was absurd, in my opinion, that the minister of defence didn't know and he said, Well, maybe he was working for us the whole time. But the minister was supposed to know about those things so as not to breed doubt and suspicion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long he worked at the Ministry of Defence as a military security officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. He was dismissed; this was in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall whether in November he still was -- it seems that you speak in the present tense, that you at that time were still employed there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He showed up later on in Australia or Canada, but don't take my word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is very far away, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's revisit briefly the conflict between Mr. Djeric and Mr. Stanisic. From June 1992 they were [as interpreted] in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And from the government minutes, it is obvious that Mr. Djeric briefed the government on the security situation and on certain specific facts on the basis of the reports that he learned at the session of the extended Presidency of which he was a member; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 28, line 25, there is an intervention in the transcript. From June 1992, Mr. Djeric was member of the extended Presidency. The transcript it just states: "... they were in the Presidency." So that line in the transcript is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, do you know that Mr. Djeric sought that the government be reconstructed first, as he stated, as early as May 1992, then in August; and for reference that will be 65 ter document 1325. Later on, in Bijeljina in September; and for reference purposes, that would be 65 ter document 1506. So on at least two, and probably three occasions, Mr. Djeric sought that the government be reconstructed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I'm not sure about May, but from the very beginning of my participation in that government, attitude on the reconstruction of the government became manifest. He wanted to increase the number of ministers and he wanted to get rid of Stanisic and somebody else, and some other people. There were numerous discussions about that. And he got a consensus from Mr. Koljevic and Madam Plavsic, but he could not obtain one from Karadzic and Krajisnik, so there were numerous discussions. Then he offered for Stanisic to remain in government as a minister without portfolio. There was different variant, and at the Assembly in Banja Luka, although he had not received Krajisnik's and Karadzic's consent, he proposed -- put forth a proposal to reconstruct the government. It was voted upon but it did not pass. And formally and legally, I thought that the whole government would fall. He did not put forward amendments to the cabinet, but a new proposal for the whole government, it was not voted in, and I thought that it had fallen, that government. But these are legal and formal things were not observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think at one point yesterday and the day before yesterday, you said that, in your view, Professor Djeric wasn't really the most suitable person to be prime minister at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he wasn't the most suitable person. He was not a man who was used to an organised and systematic mode of work. He would have had to be a very capable and crafty person. I don't want to be serious -- well, I don't want to make jokes here, but he was sort of not weasely enough. He was a university professor, so that he didn't really have the strength and the energy to resolve issues in a controversial dialogue or contradictory dialogue. It was not possible to actually conclude a conversation with him. Whenever it would come to the crux of the matter, he would just wave his hand and say, Well, you know, forget about that. So in that sense. I believe he was a very honourable man who had the best of intentions, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would suggest that we take the break now because I would like to reconsider my notes and see if I have any other questions, but I would need the break for that, and I think this is -- this would be an appropriate moment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I just wish to impart a bit of information to those of you who may not be aware of it, but I understand that efforts have been made to regulate the temperature, which we are all complaining about how close it has become in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I made a promise and I'm going to stick to the promise, so I don't have any further questions for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, due to the previous problems with the neck and spine of my client, I was asking security officer if we could just change a chair for our client and he said I should address the Chamber and with your permission they can arrange that, just instead of this one to have one of these spare chairs for him, if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Trbojevic, thank you very much. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I do have some questions on redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic. I wanted to begin by asking you something that came up very near the end of your testimony today. At page 24, line 24 -- I'm sorry, line 14, you were being asked about the Yellow Wasps, and in your answer you said: "Yes, I do recall the existence of that group, some meetings with it and when it was crushed, and those meetings were them were less than savoury. Whenever I encountered them, these were not savoury occasions." Do I take it you personally had some contacts or meetings with Yellow Wasps, and if so, could you tell the Court about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have a few contacts with them. On my way to Serbia, I was in the car, there was a check-point that they held and I would have to go through this check-point. This was in the direction of Sekovic-Karakaj communication. You couldn't get through there because there were armed men standing. They would stop your car and check your papers. And at the time we didn't have appropriate papers. We just had documents, on paper, showing that this vehicle had this VIN number and so on. We would also have a government letter and a travel voucher. And then they would check the papers, they would look at the car, search it, take away things if they thought they should, and so on. So sometimes they would even take your vehicle, or if there was a weapon, they would take that weapon away. And it wasn't very pleasant. And I heard that there were serious problems with them as well. Among other things, Velibor Ostojic, the minister, was beaten up by one of them on one such occasion. He raised his voice and asked them, Do you know who I am, I'm a minister, and then they just beat him up. And I know that there was an operation conducted by the police, a raid. They were arrested and I remember that Mr. Stanisic reported on that. He said that that thing had happened, had been conducted, and that's it. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many times you dealt with them at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About two to three times. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it all those times were before the 29th of July, 1992, when they were arrested. Do you recall approximately when those two or three times were; the earliest time, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would have had to have been before they were arrested. It had to be before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you recall what month? May, June, July?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been June. My mother was still alive then, she was in Serbia, so I went on a couple of occasions to visit her. My younger son was also staying with her, so I went on these family -- for family reasons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the time of these stops at this check-point, I take it you did not know then that these were Yellow Wasps. That's something you only learned about later, that they were Yellow Wasps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the first time they stopped me, I didn't know what they were called, but when I recounted this incident, when I told other people about this, then somebody said, Yeah, there is a group, they call themselves Yellow Wasps. And there was also this man, this Zuti and Repic, or ponytail, who I know that I saw some reports in the papers about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the time you were stopped at this check-point, who did you understand these men to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't want to intervene until this point but I didn't think this comes out of the cross-examination that I did with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It comes out of the witness's answer to a question on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is why I didn't object until this point, but I believe you are going in deep into something which was not -- what was not the object of my cross-examination. That is why I object. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It seems, Mr. Hannis, that as Mr. Zecevic has said, that when you started out, you were clearly within the ambit of his cross-examination, but your -- the details that you are now inviting the witness to speak on, you are opening up new territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I accept your ruling. I would just like to indicate for the future, that it's my position that counsel's expectation or objective in cross-examination should not determine the parameters of what is allowed on redirect. It should be based on the evidence presented by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is a new, isn't it, that's a new approach, isn't it, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not for me personally, Your Honour. It's my understanding that if a witness says something on a cross-examination, that it may not be expected or the objective of the cross-examiner, that doesn't prevent the person on redirect exploring that. This is the first I was aware that he'd had any dealings with the Yellow Wasp, and since he stated it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What the concern would be, though, is that, in the interest of time, we wouldn't wish you to go into an area which would of necessity require for the cross-examination on the new material. So if you could confine yourself to strictly what has arisen out of cross-examination, otherwise there'd be no end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I'll move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I want to take you to your testimony yesterday at page 4156, beginning at line 20, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about the Cutileiro plan. I just want to clarify: You weren't a participant in the negotiations on behalf of the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that your knowledge and information about the Cutileiro plan and any details concerning came from local media accounts and/or any general discussions and comments in and around the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 4164, line 20, Mr. Zecevic asked you about the conditions on Mount Jahorina, and he said in his question, there was no heating, no electric power, that the snow made things even worse because the roads weren't passable, you didn't have any means of communication, et cetera. And your answer was: "That's correct. We literally did not even have typewriters, no telefaxes, nothing." One of my questions is: You've seen the government sessions, the minutes from some 60 session, 61 sessions, all except for one perhaps appear to be typewritten, so there must have been a typewriter at least for the person who was typing up the minutes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were more than one, but the government did not have equipment of its own. These machines, these typewriters, were collected, taken from various companies, and at the end, we ended up with some of those assets so we could use them in work. It snowed in November already, there was a lot of snow, that's regarding the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in May, June, July, and August, there wasn't a problem with snow on Mount Jahorina, was there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a problem with electric power, but not with the snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 4174, line 19, Mr. Zecevic was asking you about the Crisis Staffs, and suggesting at the time the war commissions were being proposed, the Crisis Staffs hadn't even functioned for a month when the government concluded that measures should be taken for their abolishment. Are you aware that some of the Crisis Staffs, Serb Crisis Staffs, or SDS Crisis Staffs had been in existence since even before the conflict started, as early as January 1992? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the document that's been referred to as a Variant A and B document circulated by the SDS Main Board on the 21st of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that document as a Defence counsel here in The Hague in the Brdjanin case, when I came here for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's right. I forgot for a moment that you worked on that case. At page 4178, line 12, you were asked -- talking about the Crisis Staff, these organs that were being formed in these extraordinary circumstances suddenly became practically very powerful centres of power. And you agreed, and said: "These staffs took upon themselves the power, for example, to command military units, like a local brigade, the local police." And in the end you pointed out: "Some places it functioned harmoniously. It varied from area to area." My question was: In Pale, where the government was situated, where Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were most of the time, isn't it true that there was a local Crisis Staff in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that if you interpreted verbatim the transcript as my words in my answer to counsel Zecevic's question, I did not say that the Crisis Staff commanded either the military or the police. My reference to that was in the context of the Crisis Staff trying to have as their members people who were from their own environment including people from the police station, and this is the way that they actually exerted influence over the police or the military elements. But I didn't know any such occasions where the Crisis Staff would actually be in command of such a military unit. As for Pale, yes, there was a Crisis Staff on Pale, and I had occasion once or twice to see members of the Crisis Staff coming to speak with Mr. Krajisnik, who was the speaker of parliament, the president of the Assembly, to speak with him. And the second time, they came to meet with members of the government. So that's all I know, that members of the Crisis Staff came to visit members of the government and Mr. Krajisnik. I had occasion to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The first part of that answer you raised a question about the interpretation of your answer yesterday. I'll read you out what is in the transcript and ask you if you can confirm for me whether it's accurate or not. This is well, yesterday. I'm sorry, I don't have the updated page number. Yesterday it was page 65 -- I am sorry, page 69, which I believe is near the bottom of page 4178: "These staffs took upon themselves the power to, for example, command a military unit that was like a local brigade or a local unit. The local police, which was not local by its structure and its main system because hierarchically it was connected to the state. But practically, there were these people in the police station living in that particular area and they were subject to the authority of local power brokers. And this is now another question as to how this authority was imposed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was: Is that an accurate translation of what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit clumsy, but as I said a little earlier, I explained what I meant actually yesterday when I said that. I didn't mention yesterday another thing and maybe now I can repeat it. There's one of the municipal functions is to keep records and to issue call-up papers to conscripts. These are functions that really fall within the remit of the Ministry of Defence. However, the clerk who actually processes these is on the premises of the municipality, and this is referred to as municipal work, but they would -- when they would send these call-up papers and ask conscripts to report to the military or the police, they are not actually exercising municipal power. So this is in response to when there is someone in the Crisis Staff who would actually command or have some sort of command function in that respect. So I'm not excluding the possibility that maybe in some municipalities, the president of the Crisis Staff in co-operation or agreement with a commander of a unit would agree something that would go beyond these agreed frameworks and these envisaged frameworks, but normally that's not how it should function.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the local police chief of an SJB in a municipality with a Crisis Staff was taking directions from the Crisis Staff contrary to any direction he might be receiving through his chain of command within the MUP? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any cases where a local police commander or the chief of police actually operated contrary to orders that he would receive from the CSB or the ministry. I don't know of any such cases. As a matter of principle, he was not allowed to act in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the municipal Crisis Staffs, do you know what their composition was in terms of membership in a political party? Weren't most of the members of the Serb Crisis Staffs in April, May, June 1992, members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, probably they were, but I do know of individual instances where there were people who were brigade commanders, were chiefs of police, but were not members of the SDS. There were such cases. I do have some information about some individuals like that. But, in fact, this actually grew out of the Serb deputies who actually -- of whom most were, in fact, members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to look at Exhibit P188. This is a document that Mr. Zecevic showed you yesterday, and ask you some questions beginning at page 4186, line 7. I don't have a hard copy so hopefully we can do it on the e-court. It's a document which is apparently an instruction issued from the prime minister. I think it's signed by you and sent to the MUP. Do you recall seeing this one yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if you need the hard copy we can provide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it's one page and if he needs it I'll ask. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: The subject matter of this is requesting information about facts relating to vehicles from the TAS car factory in Vogosca and oil in Ilidza. Now, these two topics, cars from TAS and oil, those appear to be the only two matters that were ever the subject of private sessions in the government. Do you recall any other private sessions where any other subject was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a host of details that were discussed, but as for TAS vehicles, they were in the thousands so this was something that was a glaring issue, you could see it before you, and -- but the number of vehicles would just decrease and there were fewer and fewer of them, so this was a recurrent problem that was one of the most topical issues discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure you understood my question. There were only -- as far as we've seen, there were only two closed sessions or private sessions of the government. In one of those, the vehicles from TAS was discussed, and at another one, the issue about oil was discussed. My question was: Were there any other private sessions where something was discussed other than these two subjects, if you know, or if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't remember even these two closed sessions, private sessions. Whether there were any others with that indication that they are private, I don't know. It's possible, but I don't know any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And one of the reasons that those sessions would have been private, is it because there was some suspicion that high-level officials were involved with those two subject matters, the missing cars from TAS and oil in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, just a regular Joe, an insignificant person, cannot commit this kind of theft, nor can 3.000 vehicles disappear from a parking-lot without someone who was in power actually being involved, so this could not have been performed or done by just petty criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you told us yesterday that you signed this one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall why you signed it instead of Djeric? Was he just not around or was there some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably he had stepped out or gone somewhere at that point in time, so he asked me to sign it. Or maybe he just wanted to have it sent out and he was absent. There was no special reason for me signing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know why it was addressed to Ceda Kljajic personally, instead of going to Minister Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Somebody probably must have told me to do so, or maybe that's how it was written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could next look at 1D94. I think it's an MFI document at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 4191, line 25, Mr. Zecevic showed you this document and asked you about it. I think it's dated the 23rd of August, 1992. And it was sent out by the minister of the interior. I think we were unclear as to whose signature it was. But can you, from looking at the heading, can you tell me what is the nature of this document? Yesterday, Mr. Zecevic talked with you about various kinds of documents in administrative bodies, rules of procedure, instructions, decisions, orders. Can you tell, based on what you see on the screen, what kind of administrative document this was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I understood it, it was a letter. A communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did it --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A letter requesting information and pointing out that the government had concluded that it was high time to reply. This is not an official document. It's not categorised as an enactment. It's just a letter, a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what effect a request like that would have, from the minister to subordinate unit, in terms of any obligation to respond?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A reply to this could have been, Please find attached herewith a criminal report against, and then a list. The perpetrators of a criminal offence, when, where, what was the statement when questioned, then some supporting documents. It could have been a dossier, or maybe it alternatively could have been a list. We've sent this to that district prosecutor and then a list, the date and what kind of documents were sent where.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would there be any consequences to the CSB or individuals in the CSB who failed to respond to this request for information?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, this is an every-day activity, performance of every-day duties. If you fail to reply to a request for information coming from the ministry, of course that would be failing fulfill your duties. So whether that would be tantamount to grounds for disciplinary proceedings, well, that would be up to the immediate manager or responsible person to decide pursuant to the disciplinary regulations of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to next look at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to look next at Exhibit 1D96.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is one that you were shown today by Mr. Zecevic. Page 5, line 14. This is a document that appears to be a draft of-- that the government operative programme for measures to prevent social disruptions in the conditions of a state of war which was attached to a cover letter from the government secretary, Mr. Lakic. And I want to specifically ask you about an item that I think Mr. Zecevic didn't bring to your attention. It's item 26, which is found at page 14 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in e-court I think the B/C/S is at page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Hopefully you'll be able to follow this on the screen, Mr. Trbojevic. I just have one or two questions. Item 26 is translated for me as: "Agreement on exchange of prisoners of war, detainees, the wounded and the bodies of persons killed between the SR BiH" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think in the hard copy it's probably page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's item 26.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And at the end of the article it said: "This agreement, together with other documents that have already been adopted, shall serve as a basis for the work of the state commission for the exchange of POWs and detainees." I infer from that that detainees are something different and distinctive from prisoners of war, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
