utterances.text: Yes, of course I would agree with you. I see that it is reliant upon an agreement signed by the president of the SR BiH,and is expected to be signed by our side. I know that there were discussions of the International Community of the Red Cross at Geneva, that there were some agreements ensuing from those discussions, and that there were agreements subsequent to this regulating the issue of exchange of the bodies of those killed, detained, prisoners of war, evacuations, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think based on what you've said earlier in your testimony, it would be fair to interpret these detainees as being not fighters, not combatants, but civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That will be the logic of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 21, line 21, today, you were asked about whether you recall the MUP submitting on a number of occasions information on the current security situation. You said yes. You couldn't really confirm specifically because you couldn't say which of those reports you saw, but you do know that there were reports. My understanding from your prior testimony in Krajisnik and your testimony here that in spite of that, you and Djeric still felt that you weren't being fully, adequately informed by the Ministry of the Interior by the situation on the ground; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I mean, this is being made referenced to on many occasions. The gist of it was that the status of that so-called government was such that it was supposed to perform the -- a utility service which was supposed to make sure that things functioned in terms of the economy and everything else, but on the other hand, that some crucial and matters of public interest were not supposed to be on the agenda of the government. Well, to what extent we, members of the government, were to blame for failing to comprehend that and to what extent the Presidency conducted both internal and foreign affairs and limited the influence of that government, that's quite relative. It was our feeling, I can tell you, that we were constantly being marginalised or in a position which lacked importance to anybody. And there was a lot of things -- there were a lot of things going on around us and that many problems were obvious, well, that would be my feeling, which was publicly expressed on many occasions. I spoke about it in public. But this is how things went until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And since that time in 1992 until today, have you learned anything, any information that would change your opinion about whether or not you were being marginalised and under-informed by the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that after several trials here I learned many things and it's completely clear that that government was at the margins of everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 25, line 20, today, you were asked about your opinion or whether you would agree that the Ministry of the Interior, in 1992, to a great extent fulfilled what would be expected of it at that stage of being set up. You said yes, you agreed, and maybe 90 per cent, and that it functioned better than basically all the other ministries. That would suggest to me that the MUP had good communications, because wouldn't that be an essential requirement to start up an organ like the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that on two occasions partly. The infrastructure and the connectedness between police station, Security Services Centres, with the republican headquarters within the ministry of the police was, according to my impression, as far as I could divine, it worked and functioned better or more intensively than in other segments of social life. Therefore, the police were set up, minister appointed people to positions, analysed at collegium meetings what was working, what was not. There were dismissals, and simply, the impression was that that organ was functioning much better at a higher level than everybody else of us. So what they were short of, well, that's something that I cannot assess or enumerate from my position, but it is -- certainly there were some problems. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trbojevic, I don't have any further questions for the witness. I do have one procedural matter. That was a exhibit previously marked P165 and it was marked for identification but it's part of this witness's 65 ter, so I'd ask that its status change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand it's already been admitted, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand it's already been admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I said 65 ter, I meant 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, there is a matter that I would like to clarify with you in relation to the knowledge that people in your government had about detention of civilians because you told us yesterday that, in fact, you had no knowledge about detention of civilians, at least over the summer of 1992, and if I recall correctly, you told us that it wasn't until the early fall of 1992 that you were first told about detention facilities and collection points and other kinds of detention of civilians; but when you heard of it, you were told that it was all for the good of the detainees, because it was to protect them against extremists. Have I understood you correctly on this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how I put it. This is how it was, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Now, by the time you were appointed as deputy prime minister, that was in May 1992, if I recall correctly, did you understand there to be a state of armed conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I experienced in Sarajevo that shells were falling around the city, that one could be apprehended out in the street. I was arrested. I experienced a state of war, a war situation to the full, except that that I wasn't hit by any missile. So I knew that it was a war situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We are lucky that you were not hit. But who was perceived to be the enemy? Or let me put my question in another way. If there was an armed conflict as you understood it to be, then who were the parties fighting against each other? As far as you could tell, could determine at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, that war situation gradually spread like fire. Here I am sitting in Sarajevo and watching TV and seeing on TV that at the level of the republic, there were agreements being made about mixed patrols. Then I see on TV those trams burning in front of the Skenderija hall, where soldiers who were -- JNA soldiers who were leaving Sarajevo got killed. Then step by step you are drawn into a situation, you keep thinking that the very next agreement will resolve the situation, and while you wait for the next agreement, you find yourself that you cannot bear to stay there, that the situation is real and present. Then you hear about Serbian authorities going to Pale to find shelter there. Then you yourself go to Pale and you find out that there is war reigning at many places in the country. Who were the parties to the conflict? Well, the Serbs who wanted to remain in the same community with Serbia, and the Muslims, on the other hand, who wanted for Bosnia-Herzegovina to be separated. As far as the Croats and when they became a party to the conflict against either of the other two sides, well, I cannot gauge that. For a time they co-operated with the Serb side, then sometimes they fought the Muslims and then co-operated with the Muslims to fight the Serbs. That was a complicated matter. And as a civilian, you do not have any kind of inkling what is going on at the front line. You do not know anything about the military situation and then the military personnel would brief you on that military situation as per requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But am I right in understanding your testimony to be that it was generally perceived that the armed conflict was going on between the Serbs who wanted to preserve the former Yugoslavia, and the Muslims who wanted to have the Bosnia and Herzegovina become an independent and thus separate from Yugoslavia? This was what the war was all about and the enemies were the Serbs against the Muslims and perhaps the Croats? Is that how you saw it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, I understand that you are unable to tell us exactly when you first heard about detention of civilians; but what I don't understand is that when you heard of detention of a great number of civilians who were predominantly Muslim and Croats, and at the same time you knew that there was an armed conflict between Serbs and Muslims, and let's include the Croats for the sake of completion, then I would find it hard to believe that detention of civilians belonging to the enemy would be made for reasons their own protection against their own kin. And, therefore, my question to you is really this: Did you have an impression that in your government people were turning the blind eye to this information that in those detention facilities where Muslims were held, mistreatment could possibly have taken place? I'm not, Mr. Trbojevic, I'm not in any way implying that you did so, but my question is: Did it ever occur to you that there might be someone in the government who had an interest in not bringing to light what was going on in the camps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, today when I think about that it seems to me impossible for that not to be known. When I go back in my mind to that time in 1992, I know that as a normal person, it was inconceivable for me to -- for somebody to open a camp for civilians because they were of different ethnic background. And it was so among many people because the Serbs, in their history, they've experienced such camps as victims during World War II. Maybe under the influence of that, yes, but as a normal person I could not even think that somebody would deprive somebody of their liberty and put them into a camp just because they come from different ethnic background. This is the situation -- information that I got in Banja Luka, that Trnopolje was a collection centre, that the civilians [Realtime transcript read in error "Serbians"] may be put there to be protected from extremists on both sides, to spend some time there protected before they can return home, and to be protected from the Muslim side, well, it seemed logical. There was some logic to it for a time. But when on TV you first saw the footage from Trnopolje and from Manjaca, where you see a huge number of people kept there, then it became clear that we didn't know what was going on there. On the other hand, we know that the ICRC conducted talks at the republican or state level or the leadership level, trying to get an agreement for the ICRC to gain access to those camps, to list those persons, to check the living conditions there. So it was inconceivable. We had no idea that such things happened as I learned subsequently from many witnesses. I don't know, I can't [Realtime transcript read in error "can"] say that there was a person who tried to hide everything from public view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And were --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honour. Maybe I'll be of assistance. I believe the witness says I can't say that there was a person who tried to hide everything from public view. 51, 20, it says "the Serbians," which is clearly not. I think he said "the civilians." Page 51, line 20, it say that is the Serbians may be put there to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also page 51, line 23, it is Muslim side or some other side? I don't know, it's not make sense to me. Maybe our friend can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I don't know if you read English, but can you see on the screen at page 51, line 23? And are you able to understand what it says?

utterances.text: I cannot see page 51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If the interpreters would be good enough to do so. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot see LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Trbojevic, let's cut through this, I think the issue was whether or not you were being told that detained Muslim civilians were there for the protection against their own extremists, people from their own side; is that correct? Is that what you had heard?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I put it. Extremists both from their own side and from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Well, that adds an extra dimension. Moving on to my last question, you were shown today, during

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: that Mr. Stanisic had issued orders to the CSBs and the SJBs to report on all events taking place within their area of jurisdiction. And in particular to collect information and documentation about war crimes. And my question to you is: Do you know if those reports actually came? Were such reports provided on a daily basis or at least on a regular basis to the Ministry of Interior from the CSBs and the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how public security stations and centres correspond -- what was the correspondence with the ministries or the number of such reports, the level of their processing, at which intervals and by which dead-lines they were received. What I can tell you is that at the government level, we did not receive such reports. The government had no insight in such reports. I know that there was some co-operation with the war crimes institute based in Belgrade, and that that institute had collected some documentation, and from the information that I received from a judge who conducted those investigations, that documentation was forwarded to the United Nations. To whom and in what form, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanisic, when he was a minister of the interior, did he bring up that issue during any of the government meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot specifically recall him saying something at a particular government session or meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So the government was never informed by the minister of interior about the documentation of possible war crimes and the way in which such possible documentation was handled?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that my answer must be in the affirmative, meaning that I did not see such a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you don't recall Mr. Stanisic bringing it up during any meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trbojevic, for coming to assist the Tribunal. Your testimony is at an end and you are now released, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Usher, you may escort Mr. Trbojevic from the court.
